resident.chief_complaint: Progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness over 3 months, unsteady gait, and altered sensation of the feet described as 'walking on cotton wool'.
resident.history: 30-year-old male engineer of African descent presented with progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness over 3 months, associated with an unsteady gait. He reported altered sensation of his feet, described as 'walking on cotton wool'. He denied any preceding trauma and no neck or back pain.
resident.physical_exam: Normal power in both upper and lower limbs. Generalized hyper-reflexia in all muscle groups of both upper and lower limbs, bilateral inverted supinator jerk, positive Hoffman's sign, and clonus. Sensation decreased in the left sole of the foot, sparing the dorsum. Japanese Orthopaedic Association score 7; Nurick's Grading grade 3.
key_positive_signs: Generalized hyper-reflexia in all muscle groups of both upper and lower limbs
Decreased sensation in the left sole of the foot sparing the dorsum
MRI stenosis with cord signal changes C4-C6 from bony growth at C6 spinous process
resident.past_history: Denied any preceding trauma; no neck or back pain. No other past medical history documented.
resident.public_message: A 30-year-old male of African descent presented with progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness over 3 months, unsteady gait, and altered sensation of the feet described as 'walking on cotton wool'. Examination revealed normal power but generalized hyper-reflexia, bilateral inverted supinator jerk, positive Hoffman's sign, clonus, and decreased sensation in the left sole sparing the dorsum. JOA score was 7 and Nurick's grade 3. MRI of the whole spine showed stenosis with cord signal changes from C4 to C6 secondary to impingement by a bony growth from the C6 spinous process; CT confirmed the bony mass. These findings are reported as recorded.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description only; the films were not available for review. The record describes spinal canal stenosis with cord signal changes from C4-6 due to dorsal canal impingement by a prominent bony growth arising anterosuperiorly from the C6 spinous process. The record does not provide a stenosis grade. These findings correlate highly with the reported cervical myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical myelopathy involving upper motor neuron pathways secondary to C4-C6 dorsal cord compression; additional left S1-distribution sensory deficit suggests possible coexisting lumbosacral radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy.

red_flags.finding: Reported progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness with normal power on examination.
red_flags.rationale: The reported weakness is not supported by objective motor examination; this may reflect subjective fatigue, early myelopathy without measurable power loss, or functional overlay. It does not offer an alternative explanation for the upper motor neuron signs and does not change the indication from cervical cord compression.

red_flags.finding: Decreased sensation in the left sole of the foot sparing the dorsum.
red_flags.rationale: This sensory pattern is not typical of cervical cord myelopathy (which would be bilateral or below a level) and suggests a peripheral process such as left S1 radiculopathy or distal neuropathy. It coexists rather than altering the cervical localization or indication.

red_flags.finding: JOA score 7 and Nurick grade 3 despite documented normal power in all limbs.
red_flags.rationale: The severe functional scores conflict with the normal motor examination. This discrepancy may indicate non-organic factors, cognitive/coordination issues, or imprecise scoring, but it does not negate the myelopathic signs. It warrants further clarification but does not change the causal role of the C4-C6 compression.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The C4-C6 dorsal compression and cord signal change explain the upper motor neuron signs, but the unilateral left sole sensory loss sparing the dorsum is not explained by this lesion; it suggests a coexisting left S1 or peripheral nerve process.
neurology.public_message: Localization is to the cervical spinal cord at C4-C6, matching the upper motor neuron findings. The imaging explains the dominant myelopathic syndrome. Red flags: (1) reported weakness but normal power — coexisting, does not change indication; (2) left S1-distribution sensory loss — coexisting, likely peripheral/radicular; (3) JOA 7/Nurick 3 with normal power — coexisting, needs clarification. Symptom-imaging mismatch: left sole sensory loss is not explained by cervical lesion.

physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3 months initial, extendable to 6 months if stable or improving
preconditions_for_failure: Any decline in JOA score or Nurick grade during the trial
Appearance of new or worsening objective neurologic deficits (e.g., motor weakness, gait deterioration)
No improvement or stabilization of myelopathic symptoms after 3 months of structured rehabilitation
Progression of cord signal change on follow-up MRI at 3 months
Patient preference for surgery after informed discussion
physiatrist_opening.public_message: As the rehabilitation physician, I formally propose a conservative management trial: 3 months (extendable to 6 if stable or improving) of supervised physical therapy focused on gait, balance, core stabilization, and posture; activity modification; and close neurologic monitoring. The reported success rate for severe cervical myelopathy with cord signal change is modest (~30%), and I acknowledge the evidence that progressive myelopathy may warrant early surgical decompression to prevent irreversible cord damage. Therefore, this trial is only appropriate with strict preconditions: any decline in JOA/Nurick, new neurologic deficits, or progression of MRI signal change mandates immediate surgical referral. I am not yet persuaded that surgery must be the first step for this young patient, but I will concede if these conditions are met.

physiatrist_final.proposed_duration: 3 months initial, extendable to 6 months if stable or improving

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director emphasizes the risk of irreversible cord injury from progressive myelopathy with cord signal change. I agree these are serious, and that is exactly why my proposal includes strict failure criteria: any decline in JOA/Nurick, new deficits, or MRI progression triggers immediate surgical referral. However, he has not identified a finding I have underweighted; cord signal change and progression are already central to my decision to make the trial conditional. In a 30-year-old with normal power and JOA 7, a 3-month structured conservative trial with close monitoring remains a reasonable option, not a delay, because it either improves function or quickly crosses the threshold for surgery. I maintain my conditional stance.

vice_opinions.assessment: This 30-year-old patient presents with progressive cervical myelopathy (JOA 7, Nurick 3) and documented cord signal change from C4 to C6 caused by dorsal bony compression from a C6 spinous process lesion. Although motor power is recorded as normal, the combination of hyperreflexia, inverted supinator jerk, Hoffman's sign, and clonus indicates significant upper motor neuron dysfunction. The left sole sensory loss is not explained by the cervical lesion and likely represents a coexisting peripheral or lumbosacral process, but it does not alter the primary surgical indication. In progressive myelopathy with cord signal change, early surgical decompression is the standard of care to prevent irreversible cord damage. A prolonged conservative trial, as proposed by rehabilitation, carries an unacceptable risk of neurologic deterioration and is not advisable as the initial strategy.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical decompression (C4-C6 laminectomy or laminoplasty) with excision of the bony mass arising from the C6 spinous process, and instrumented fusion if facet joints are compromised or instability is present.
Posterior decompression with laminoplasty alone, preserving motion, if the mass can be fully resected without significant destabilization.
Short preoperative optimization with physiotherapy and close neurologic monitoring, followed by surgical decompression within 2-4 weeks if no improvement.
Conservative management trial as proposed by the rehabilitation physician, with strict monitoring and immediate surgical referral on any decline (not preferred).
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical decompression (C4-C6 laminectomy or laminoplasty) with excision of the bony mass from the C6 spinous process, adding instrumented fusion if instability is present or created.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the rehabilitation physician's proposal for a 3-month conservative trial as the first step. In progressive cervical myelopathy with cord signal change, evidence strongly favors early decompression; a trial risks irreversible neurologic decline.

The discrepancy between reported weakness and normal motor power needs clarification before finalizing surgical urgency. If objective weakness is absent, the JOA score may overstate myelopathy severity, but cord compression remains clear and still warrants surgery.

The left sole sensory loss is unexplained by the C4-C6 lesion. Electrodiagnostic studies (EMG/NCS) should be considered to evaluate for a concurrent lumbosacral radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy, which could affect perioperative positioning and outcome expectations.

The exact nature of the bony mass is not fully characterized. Preoperative advanced imaging (e.g., MRI with contrast) and possibly CT-guided biopsy may be needed to rule out an aggressive or malignant lesion, which could alter surgical strategy.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that dynamic flexion-extension radiographs and additional MRI sequences should be obtained before scheduling surgery to assess stability and lesion characteristics?
Should we proceed directly to surgery after necessary workup, or allow a short period of preoperative medical optimization while the patient is hospitalized?
For this young patient, would you favor a laminectomy with instrumented fusion or a laminoplasty if the posterior elements can be preserved? Your preference will guide the operative plan.
How would you like to coordinate the unexplained left sole sensory loss—should neurology perform EMG/NCS preoperatively, or can this be deferred until after cervical decompression?
vice_opinions.public_message: I recommend early surgical decompression as the primary approach for this patient. The progressive cervical myelopathy with C4-C6 cord signal change secondary to dorsal bony compression warrants posterior decompression and excision of the mass, with fusion or laminoplasty decided based on intraoperative stability. I do not support a prolonged conservative trial because of the risk of irreversible cord injury. We should clarify the left sole sensory finding and better characterize the bony lesion, but these issues should not delay surgical intervention.

director_rulings.final_decision: Close this meeting for additional workup. Surgery is indicated as things stand, but we require dynamic flexion-extension radiographs, contrast-enhanced MRI with additional sequences to characterize the C6 spinous process lesion, and EMG/NCS of the lower limbs to evaluate the unexplained left S1 sensory loss. We will reconvene once these results are available. If the imaging suggests an aggressive or malignant lesion, or if dynamic studies reveal instability, the surgical strategy will be adjusted accordingly (including possible extended resection and instrumented fusion). If EMG/NCS shows significant peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy, we will modify perioperative positioning and outcome expectations. The anesthesiologist must complete an airway assessment before any surgery.
delegated_tasks: Radiologist: perform and report dynamic flexion-extension radiographs and contrast-enhanced MRI with additional sequences (e.g., STIR, T1 post-contrast); provide a differential for the bony lesion and comment on instability.
Neurologist: arrange EMG/NCS of the lower limbs and correlate the left S1 distribution sensory loss with the cervical findings.
Anesthesiologist: perform and document a full airway assessment and a plan for safe prone positioning.
Resident: coordinate scheduling of the ordered tests and ensure the patient's consent for diagnostic procedures is obtained.
Vice Director: review the completed workup and prepare a detailed surgical plan (laminectomy vs laminoplasty, need for fusion) for the next meeting.
Physiatrist: provide preoperative baseline functional assessments and outline postoperative rehabilitation goals, contingent on surgery.
director_rulings.reason_for_delay: Required workup to characterize the bony lesion, assess spinal stability, and clarify the unexplained left S1 sensory loss before finalizing the surgical approach.
